title: Fibrewise ampleness criterion for cubical lines on semiabelian schemes
statement: Let $T$ be a normal locally Noetherian scheme [def-pc-scheme, pqf-def-locnoeth], where normal means that every local ring is an integrally closed domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Let $p:H\to T$ be a smooth separated commutative group scheme of finite presentation [def-pc-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. Its addition, inverse $\iota$ and identity $e$ are $T$-morphisms satisfying the commutative group identities, and separated means that the diagonal is a closed immersion. Assume its geometric fibres are semiabelian [def-sfb-semiabelian-geometric-fibres]. Let $(B,r,\tau)$ be a cubical rigidified line on $H$ [def-sfb-cubical-rigidified-line]. In particular $B$ is an invertible module [def-sc-invertible-module], with $r:e^*B\simeq\mathcal O_T$ and a normalized permutation-invariant cube trivialization satisfying the cube cocycle identity. All line pullbacks are tensor inverse images [def-pc-module-pullback]. For each $t\in T$, let $H_t=H\times_T\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t)$ be the residue-field fibre [def-pc-fibre-product, def-weil-residue-field] and $B_t$ the pulled-back line. If $B_t$ is ample for every $t\in T$ [def-weil-pbc-ample-invertible-module], then for every affine open $V\subseteq T$, the restriction $B|_{p^{-1}(V)}$ is ample. No generic ampleness or symmetry hypothesis is imposed, and $p$ need not be proper.

source.place: XI, fibrewise-to-relative positivity input for cubical lines; original local WANTED. Agent-formulated supporting criterion, not the proper-morphism ample-neighbourhood lemma. No precise numbered Raynaud lemma is asserted without the original.

proof.text: Fix an affine open $V\subseteq T$ and $t\in V$. Put $A=\mathcal O_{T,t}$. Normality gives that $A$ is an integrally closed domain. A Noetherian affine chart around $t$ presents $A$ as a localization of a Noetherian ring, so it is Noetherian by the localization lemma. Pull back $H,B,r,\tau$ to $\operatorname{Spec}A$. Smoothness, separatedness and finite presentation persist by the cited base-change statements, and the group identities persist by pulling back their commuting diagrams. Every residue fibre here is the corresponding original residue fibre at a generalization of $t$; in particular its line is ample. Semiabelian geometric fibres and the cubical structure persist by their definitions. Choose a separable closure of $\kappa(t)$ and put $R=A^{\mathrm{sh}}$, $X=H_R$, $L=B_R$. The triples lemma makes $R$ a strictly henselian local ring, and the strict-henselization Noetherian lemma makes it Noetherian.

source.place: Agent proof: cubical fibrewise ampleness supporting the relative Picard input

proof.text: Apply the strict-local affine-seed lemma to the $A$-family, using ampleness at every prime of $A$, to obtain $n\geq1$ and $s\in\Gamma(X,L^n)$ with $U=X_s$ affine and containing the closed identity. The rigidification identifies $e_R^*L^n$ with $\mathcal O_R$. Thus $e_R^*s$ is an element of $R$ outside its maximal ideal and hence a unit. Consequently the WHOLE identity section factors through $U$, so $U_\Omega$ is nonempty for every geometric fibre. The scheme $X$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated since it is of finite presentation over the affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}R$.

source.place: Agent proof: cubical fibrewise ampleness supporting the relative Picard input

proof.text: Every geometric fibre of $X$ is connected: in its semiabelian presentation the split torus and the abelian variety are connected; a clopen decomposition of the middle group is constant on each torus coset, descends along the fppf quotient to a clopen decomposition of the abelian variety, and is therefore constant. Applying the smooth-section component lemma, its open subfamily contains every point of every fibre, since all those fibres are connected; hence that open is $X$. Thus all residue fibres of $X$ are geometrically irreducible. The section-density lemma now applies to $X/R$: the values of $X(R)$ meet every nonempty open of each geometric fibre. All its hypotheses hold: $R$ is Noetherian strictly henselian, $X/R$ is smooth separated of finite presentation, and it has the identity section.

source.place: Agent proof: cubical fibrewise ampleness supporting the relative Picard input

proof.text:
For any $a\in X(R)$ write $t_a(x)=x+a$. Pull the trivialized cube $\Theta_3(L)$ back along $x\mapsto(x,a,-a)$. Its factors are $L$ at $x$ twice, $L$ at $a,-a$, the inverse factors at $x+a,x-a,0$, and the inverse factor at $0$. Cancelling the identity factors with the rigidification gives
$t_a^*L\otimes t_{-a}^*L\simeq L^2\otimes p_R^*(a^*L\otimes(-a)^*L)$.
An invertible module on the local scheme $\operatorname{Spec}R$ is trivial: a trivializing open containing its closed point is the whole scheme. Choose a trivialization of the base factor. Tensoring the displayed isomorphism $n$ times transports $t_a^*s\otimes t_{-a}^*s$ to a section $q_a\in\Gamma(X,L^{2n})$. The pullback and tensor fibre formulas show exactly that $X_{q_a}=t_a^{-1}(U)\cap t_{-a}^{-1}(U)$. No symmetry of $L$ is used.

source.place: Agent proof: cubical fibrewise ampleness supporting the relative Picard input

proof.text:
The open $t_a^{-1}(U)$ is affine because translation is an isomorphism. Intersect it with the nonvanishing locus of the section $t_{-a}^*s$ of $t_{-a}^*L^n$; the affine-cap-section lemma makes $X_{q_a}$ affine. To see these opens cover $X$, take a geometric point $x$ of any fibre $X_\Omega$. The possible translation parameters form the open
$W_x=(U_\Omega-x)\cap(x-U_\Omega)\subset X_\Omega$.
Both terms are nonempty opens, as $U_\Omega$ contains the identity and translation/inversion are automorphisms. Geometric irreducibility makes $W_x$ nonempty. Section density gives $a\in X(R)$ with $a_\Omega\in W_x$. Then $x+a_\Omega$ and $x-a_\Omega$ lie in $U_\Omega$, so $x\in X_{q_a}$. Every scheme point admits a geometric point above it, so these opens cover all points of $X$. The quasi-compactness from step 2 and these positive-power global sections with affine nonvanishing opens give ampleness of $L$ by the definition.

source.place: Agent proof: cubical fibrewise ampleness supporting the relative Picard input

proof.text: Use the small cofiltered category of affine pointed etale neighbourhoods of the chosen geometric point over $t\in V$. Its limit is $\operatorname{Spec}R$ by the strict-henselization limit construction (the affine strict-local ring comparison identifies this limit with the algebraic strict henselization of $\mathcal O_{V,t}$, respecting the map to $V$). Each neighbourhood $W_i$ is affine. Inverse images $H_i=H\times_TW_i$ are quasi-compact and quasi-separated by finite presentation; every transition is affine, being a base change of a map between affine schemes. Their limit is $X$: a compatible family of maps to $H_i$ is precisely a map to $H$ together with a compatible family to $W_i$, and the latter uniquely gives a map to $\operatorname{Spec}R$. Reindex this small cofiltered diagram by a nonempty directed set as in the reindexing lemma; the terms and affine transitions are unchanged. The line on any chosen stage is the pullback of $B$, with pullback $L$ on the limit. The ample limit-descent lemma therefore supplies an affine pointed etale neighbourhood $W_t\to V$ on which $B|_{H_{W_t}}$ is ample.

source.place: Agent proof: cubical fibrewise ampleness supporting the relative Picard input

proof.text: For every affine open $W'\subseteq W_t$, its inclusion into the affine scheme $W_t$ is affine (on affine schemes it is induced by the corresponding ring map). Its base change $H_{W'}\to H_{W_t}$ is affine, so the ample pullback lemma makes $B|_{H_{W'}}$ ample. The pointed neighbourhoods $W_t\to V$ for all $t\in V$ form a jointly surjective etale family. Apply the ample-local lemma in its scheme case to $H_V\to V$ and this family: it gives ampleness over the inverse image of every affine open of $V$, including $V$ itself. Since $V\subseteq T$ was arbitrary, this proves the asserted relative ampleness. For $V$ empty the assertion follows directly from the ample definition.
